Phishing and Fake Invoices: A Plain-English Checklist for Small Businesses

Phishing is still the most common cyber attack on UK businesses. Here is how to spot the usual tricks, the few habits that stop most of them, and exactly where to report a suspicious message.

By Gibson Nyendwa · 4 November 2026 · 3 min read

On this page

  1. How common is it?
  2. What phishing usually looks like
  3. Five habits that stop most of it
  4. Where to report a suspicious message
  5. If someone has already clicked or paid
  6. My view

If you run a small business, the cyber attack you are most likely to meet is not a hacker breaking through a firewall. It is an email, a text or a phone call that looks ordinary and asks you to do something quickly: pay an invoice, confirm a login, update some bank details.

This guide is for owners and staff of small firms, charities and sole traders. It explains what phishing usually looks like, the habits that stop most of it, and what to do if someone has already clicked. It is defensive advice only, and it does not replace help from a professional during a live incident.

How common is it?

The UK Government's Cyber Security Breaches Survey 2025/26, published on 30 April 2026, found that 43% of businesses had experienced a cyber security breach or attack in the previous 12 months. Phishing was by far the most common type, experienced by 38% of businesses. Small firms are not left alone because they are small: the survey put the figure at 42% for micro businesses and 46% for small ones.

What phishing usually looks like

Most phishing relies on a handful of pressures rather than clever technology. Watch for these:

  • Urgency or fear: an overdue payment, a suspended account, a parcel that cannot be delivered, a deadline today.
  • A change of bank details from a supplier, often arriving just before an invoice is due.
  • A login page you reach from a link rather than by typing the address yourself.
  • A sender that is nearly right: a familiar name with an odd email address, or a domain with one letter changed.
  • Requests to keep it quiet, to buy gift cards, or to bypass your usual way of approving payments.

None of these proves a message is fake, and real messages can be clumsy. The point is to pause when you see them, not to become an expert in spotting forgeries.

Five habits that stop most of it

  • Check any change of bank details by phone, using a number you already hold for that supplier, never one in the email asking for the change.
  • Go direct. If an email says your account needs attention, close it and open the website or app yourself.
  • Turn on two-step verification for email, banking and accounting software. It means a stolen password on its own is not enough.
  • Keep devices and software updated, and back up the files your business could not work without.
  • Agree a simple rule with staff: anyone can question a payment request, and nobody gets in trouble for checking.

These match the advice in the National Cyber Security Centre's Small Business Guide, which is free and worth reading in full. If you want a recognised baseline, the government-backed Cyber Essentials scheme sets out basic technical controls and offers certification.

Where to report a suspicious message

Reporting takes seconds and helps take scam sites down. The official routes are:

  • Emails: forward them to report@phishing.gov.uk. The NCSC investigates them.
  • Texts: forward them to 7726. It is free and goes to your mobile network.
  • Adverts: report misleading adverts to the Advertising Standards Authority, or to the search engine that showed them.

If someone has already clicked or paid

Act quickly and do not be embarrassed. People who report early limit the damage.

  • If money has gone, call your bank straight away using the number on your card or statement.
  • In England and Wales, report fraud to Report Fraud online at reportfraud.police.uk or on 0300 123 2040. In Scotland, report it to Police Scotland.
  • If a password was entered on a fake page, change it, and change it anywhere else you used the same one. Check that two-step verification is still switched on.
  • If customer or staff personal data may have been exposed, read the ICO's guidance on responding to a personal data breach. Some breaches must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours.

My view

In my experience the businesses that cope best are not the ones with the most expensive software. They are the ones where checking is normal: where a quick phone call to confirm bank details is just how things are done. That habit costs nothing and protects you from the attack you are most likely to face.
